title: My Parents Gave My Wedding Venue to My Sister—Then the Manager Opened the Contract
excerpt: I knew something was wrong the moment my mother called me on Tuesday morning.Not because she sounded nervous.She didn't.She sounded completely calm.Almost cheer...
author: Admin

blocks.text: I knew something was wrong the moment my mother called me on Tuesday morning.
“Sweetheart,” she said, “I just wanted to let you know that the country club has been given to Vanessa.”
I was standing in my kitchen, holding a mug of coffee.
For several seconds, I didn’t understand what she meant.
I stared at the wedding binder sitting on my counter.
The one with my name and Caleb’s name printed across the front.
The one I had carried around for eight months.
The one filled with seating charts, vendor numbers, menu samples, flower arrangements, and a dozen different versions of the same table plan.
“The ballroom I reserved for my wedding?” I asked.
Because I couldn’t believe she was serious.
“And the deposit has already been paid.”
“Then what exactly does ‘given to Vanessa’ mean?”
Then she said the sentence that made my stomach drop.
“Your sister’s wedding is more important right now.”
Caleb and I had spent months planning our wedding.
The country club ballroom had been perfect.
And a long wall of glass overlooking the gardens.
I’d fallen in love with it the first time I saw it.
So when my mother said they had “given” it to my sister, I assumed there had to be some misunderstanding.
When I arrived at the country club that afternoon, the parking lot was already full.
Standing beneath the chandeliers as though the entire ballroom had been built for her.
A wedding planner stood beside her with a clipboard.
My father was on the other side of the room carrying boxes of decorations.
My father walked toward me carrying a large cardboard box.
“Quit staring,” he said. “Start decorating.”
Inside were rolls of ribbon, artificial flowers, candles, and table decorations.
“You want me to decorate my sister’s wedding?”
“No. She told me you gave it to Vanessa.”
“You can’t give someone something you don’t own.”
“Why are you always making everything about yourself?”
The venue manager, Mr. Harris, was standing near the entrance.
“Whose name is on the contract—and who paid the deposit?”
My father put down the box he was holding.
A minute later, Mr. Harris returned with a thick folder.
“I’m sorry,” he said, “but I think there has been a serious misunderstanding.”
“The ballroom is reserved under her name.”
“That doesn’t matter. We’re her parents.”
“The contract was signed by her. The deposit was paid by her. The remaining balance is scheduled according to her payment agreement.”
“I understand. But you don’t have a reservation here.”
I could see the anger building in her eyes.
Then my father said something I’ll never forget.
“You’re really going to let your sister lose her wedding because of a piece of paper?”
“She lost it because you promised her something that wasn’t yours to promise.”
“The contract contains a non-transfer clause.”
“It means the reservation cannot simply be transferred to another person.”
“And the person who signed the contract has exclusive authority over the booking.”
They wanted me to become the villain in their story.
“The reservation stays exactly as it is.”
That evening, my mother called seventeen times.
Apparently, the story had already spread.
According to my mother, I had “destroyed my sister’s wedding.”
According to my aunt, I was “holding a grudge over a silly venue.”
According to my cousin, I should “be the bigger person.”
“Did your parents know you paid the deposit?”
“Then why would they think they could give it away?”
Why would my parents confidently promise my wedding venue to Vanessa?
Why would they assume I would simply surrender?
The next morning, I received an email from the country club.
